title: Under the fig tree (John 1:43–51)
hook: Nathanael scoffs, can anything good come from Nazareth? and is seen before he's met

segments.voice: Yesterday, two disciples followed, and Jesus asked what they were looking for. Your line was come and see. Who did you invite to something you love? Day five hundred ninety-six.

Everybody has a town they make jokes about. The place you drive through without stopping. The place with the accent. Philip has just met Jesus, and he runs to find his friend Nathanael, bursting with it: we've found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about. Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. And Nathanael answers, in the King James words: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" Nazareth was a small village in Galilee. The Hebrew scriptures never mention it at all. And Philip doesn't argue. He just borrows Jesus's words from yesterday: come and see.

So Nathanael comes, probably still skeptical. And before he can say a word, Jesus sees him coming and says: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!" No guile: nothing fake, no hidden angle. Nathanael has just insulted Jesus's hometown, and Jesus compliments his honesty. Nathanael is thrown. How do you know me? And Jesus answers: "Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee." Nobody knows what Nathanael was doing under that fig tree. John doesn't say. Some readers think of the prophets' picture of peace, everyone sitting under their own vine and fig tree. Some point to later Jewish writings that picture teachers studying under fig trees. The honest answer is that we don't know, and that seems to be the point: something private, something only Nathanael would know about, and Jesus saw it. Nathanael's skepticism collapses into the biggest confession so far in the Gospel: "Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel." And Jesus, almost amused: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You'll see greater things than these. You'll see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. That's Jacob's ladder from Genesis, the dream where angels go up and down between heaven and earth. Jacob, the man famous for guile, meets the man with none. And the man who made the Nazareth joke ends up seeing heaven open.
screen: `AN ISRAELITE IN WHOM IS NO GUILE.`
`I SAW THEE UNDER THE FIG TREE.`
then, large: `CAN THERE ANY GOOD THING COME OUT OF NAZARETH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a place you scorn a chance. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place, a group, or a kind of person you've written off with a joke. A town, a neighborhood, a school, a profession, a political side. Notice the line you usually say about them. Now imagine being taken there by a friend who says, just come and see. Picture one good thing you might find. Hold it a moment. If you pray, you can ask to see people the way Nathanael was seen. The bell holds the time.
Under the fig tree. Where Jesus saw Nathanael before they met: a private moment, known to God, that turned a skeptic into a believer.
Your line: can anything good come? Today, notice when you write off a place or a group, and look for one good thing from there instead. Day five hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Many Christians identify Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew and honor him on his feast day, and the call of Nathanael is often read in the season after Epiphany.

fork.setup: you're Philip. you tell your friend you've found the one the prophets wrote about, and he sneers: from Nazareth? what do you say?
fork.reveal: Philip doesn't argue. "come and see." and when Nathanael comes, Jesus already knows him.

original.note: Hebrew: Nathanael, 'God has given'. the name appears in John's Gospel only.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus had a sort of supernatural vision of a man under a tree.
what it means: a skeptic who mocked Nazareth is seen and known before he's met, and ends up confessing the Son of God.
what a scholar hears: 'no guile' and the angels ascending and descending echo Jacob, who was known for deceit (Genesis 27; 28:12); and what the fig tree meant is genuinely unknown.

notes: Fig tree readings: Micah 4:4 (vine and fig tree as a picture of peace); later rabbinic stories of study under fig trees. Both given as possibilities; the text is silent.
Nazareth not mentioned in the Hebrew Bible, Josephus or the Talmud: commonly stated; the script says only the Hebrew scriptures. Confirm.
Nathanael identified with Bartholomew by tradition (feast August 24 in the West). Confirm phrasing in howItsDone.
Hebrew נְתַנְאֵל 'God has given' (e.g. Numbers 1:8). Confirm.
